FLM inference demo

Type a prompt, generate a story, then click any word piece to see the five most likely alternatives at that point and the fuzzy rules that pushed it. Everything runs in this browser tab: the weights (about 400 KB per model) are downloaded once and generation happens in JavaScript on your device, with no server.

layerrulegateeffectthe rule's strongest pushes

Effect is the rule's signed share of this token's score. A rule's strongest pushes are the pieces it raises most overall, not necessarily this token: the model's prediction is the sum of many rules.

Brain surgery: say what should have come next

Pick the piece that should have followed here. The page finds the smallest change to the strongest rules of the last block that makes it the top choice, shows you exactly what it would change, and applies it only when you press Apply. Undo restores the weights exactly. The change is to this page's copy of the model and is gone when you reload.

Edits as JSON (export, or paste to apply)

What we measured on the default model (PLAN_SURGERY.md): such an edit fixed 97 of 100 near misses and 56 of 100 far misses, but changed the top prediction at about 2% of other places where the same rules fire (8% to 10% for far misses), and where the same rules fire in other stories 30% of the previously right predictions broke. You can see exactly what you changed and take it back; the edit is not free of side effects.

How this model is built

Rule timeline: which fuzzy rules fired for each piece

Rows are the 14 rules with the largest total effect over this text; columns are the generated pieces. Teal means the rule's gate was positive, orange negative; stronger colour is a larger gate. Click a rule's label to see its membership functions, or a column to pick that piece above.

Most used rules

Rules are ranked by how often each is the strongest at a position, over 48 validation windows. The pieces listed are the ones the rule raises most. Click a rule to inspect it.

Each panel is one of the 16 input dimensions of this rule. The curve is the rule's membership function on that dimension (its centre and width); the rule's firing is the product of these 16 curves. Gray bars show where the data falls on that dimension; teal bars show where it falls when this rule fires strongly. Panels are ordered from most to least selective (data spread divided by membership width): a high value means the rule only accepts a narrow part of the data on that dimension.

Where it fires most

What to expect

The 14M option (140 times larger than the others, 0.668 bits per character) is a separate download of 14 MB the first time you select it. The other models are tiny (about 100 thousand parameters) trained only on simple children's stories (TinyStories). All three have every block component built from fuzzy inference systems: the causal convolution, the normalisation, the gates, the feed-forward rules and the attention-like projections. The first is the strongest and uses a new embedding shape found by a search over vocabulary size, head size and block width: a vocabulary of 6,144 word pieces, 640 of them with full-width crisp embeddings and the rest as fuzzy sets over eight prototypes, and blocks of width 32. It reaches 0.952 bits per character after 300 million characters of training plus a short low-rate final phase (the better of two training runs), against 0.928 for the hybrid recipe at its own best shape and schedule given the same final phase, about 2.6% worse. The second is the earlier best shape trained on 1 billion characters (0.974, the better of two runs); the third is the same earlier model after 300 million characters (0.987). In blind ratings (two raters, 32 stories each, made before the final phase) the new model scored about 7.1 out of 15 for coherence, the same as the hybrid and the earlier fuzzy models (7.3 to 7.6) within the noise of the ratings. By default the sampler discourages repeated phrases (a rule called DRY: about half as many repeated word triples, the same rated coherence); a checkbox turns it off. They write fluent, short, childlike sentences, then often drift, repeat or lose the plot after a few sentences. They know nothing outside that story world, and nothing here is reviewed for accuracy. The seeded sampler is JavaScript's, so a seed does not reproduce the Python runs in the write-up.

Source, training scripts and results: experiments/fuzzy-language-model in the grad-school repository (WRITEUP.md). Everything on this page runs on your device; nothing you type is sent anywhere.
